According to Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K, the following fiscal 2024 results (compared with fiscal 2023) were reported as unfavorably affected by the weakness of foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar:

1. **Greater China net sales** — Greater China net sales decreased 8% year over year, and the weakness in the **renminbi** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on the segment's net sales during 2024.

2. **Japan net sales** — The weakness in the **yen** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Japan net sales during 2024 (segment sales still rose 3%).

Here are the figures Boeing's 2025 Form 10-K gives regarding IAM District 837:

## The 2025 IAM District 837 Strike

- **Employee count — approximately 3,200 employees**: This is the number of Boeing employees at the company's St. Louis area sites (Missouri) who are represented by IAM District 837, as stated in the Human Capital section (Item 1, p. 2 of the filing). The MD&A Overview (p. 24) repeats that IAM 837 represents "approximately 3,200 Boeing employees."

- **Duration — 101 days**: From the Human Capital section — "During 2025, employees represented by IAM District 837... went out on strike for 101 days, disrupting our St. Louis operations and impacting programs including F/A-18, F-15, T-7A, MQ-25 and Weapons."

- **Calendar dates — August 4, 2025 and November 13, 2025**: From the MD&A Overview — the work stoppage was "initiated on August 4, 2025" and ended on "November 13, 2025," when IAM 837 members "voted to ratify a new contract thereby ending the work stoppage."

## The Current Collective Bargaining Agreement with IAM District 837

- **Expiration date — July 2030**: In the Human Capital section's table of principal collective bargaining agreements, the row for IAM District 837 (principal location: Missouri) lists an expiration date of July 2030. This is the expiration of the current (newly ratified) agreement between Boeing and IAM District 837.

## Summary of What Each Refers To

| Figure | What it refers to |
|---|---|
| ~3,200 employees | Size of the IAM District 837-represented workforce at Boeing's St. Louis area sites |
| 101 days | Length of the 2025 strike by IAM 837-represented employees |
| August 4, 2025 | Date the IAM 837 work stoppage began |
| November 13, 2025 | Date IAM 837 members ratified a new contract, ending the strike |
| July 2030 | Expiration date of Boeing's current collective bargaining agreement with IAM District 837 (Missouri) |

For context, the filing also notes the strike disrupted St. Louis operations and impacted the F/A-18, F-15, T-7A Red Hawk, MQ-25, and Weapons programs, and it contrasts this with the separate 2024 strike by IAM District 751 (over 30,000 employees, 53 days, ended November 4, 2024).

Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K (excluding exhibits) gives four dollar amounts for dividends on the 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock ("Mandatory convertible preferred stock"):

**$72 million — dividends declared in December 2024**
- Note 19 (Shareholders' Equity) states: "In December 2024, dividends of $72 [million] were declared to holders of record as of January 1, 2025... and were paid in cash on January 15, 2025."
- The Consolidated Statements of Equity also reflect this as "Cash dividends declared on Mandatory convertible preferred stock ($72)."

**$12.50 per share — the per-share amount of that declared dividend**
- From the same sentence in Note 19: the $72 million declared "represent[s] $12.50 per share." This is the quarterly 6.00% annual rate applied for the initial dividend period (the stock was issued October 31, 2024, so the first payment covered roughly one quarter).

**$58 million — dividends accumulated during 2024 (used in EPS)**
- The Consolidated Statements of Operations and the segment data summary deduct "Mandatory convertible preferred stock dividends accumulated during the period" of $58 million from net loss attributable to Boeing shareholders to arrive at net loss attributable to Boeing common shareholders ($11,875 million). Note 4 (Earnings Per Share) uses the same $58 million figure in the basic/diluted loss-per-share computation. It represents the cumulative dividends accrued from the October 31, 2024 issuance through December 31, 2024 (the portion attributable to 2024 earnings allocation).

**Up to $345 million per year — expected annual cash requirement**
- In the "Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity" section (Item 1A), Boeing states it "expect[s] to require up to $345 million of cash per year for the payment of dividends on the outstanding shares of [the] 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock... through the mandatory conversion date of October 15, 2027." This is the full annual dividend on the 5,750,000 outstanding preferred shares (6.00% × $1,000 liquidation preference × 5.75 million shares = $345 million), assuming cash payment each year.

In summary: $72 million (declared December 2024, paid January 15, 2025), $12.50 per share (per-share amount of that declaration), $58 million (accumulated during 2024 for EPS purposes), and up to $345 million per year (anticipated annual cash dividends through the October 15, 2027 mandatory conversion date).

In Apple's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (Item 3, Legal Proceedings, and the related regulatory-scrutiny risk factor), five developments are dated to a specific day or month of calendar year 2025:

**April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act, Article 5(4) Investigation**
The European Commission fined Apple €500 million and issued a cease-and-desist order requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed the decision.

**April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act, Article 6(4) Investigation**
Also on that date, the Commission issued preliminary findings in its separate investigation into whether Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces violate the DMA. A final violation determination could bring a cease-and-desist order and fines up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales.

**April 30, 2025 — Epic Games litigation**
The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 Injunction and enjoined it from: imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app; restricting, conditioning, limiting, or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to outside purchases; or otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app. The court also denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate.

**September 2, 2025 — Google search antitrust remedies (commercial partner matter)**
Following the August 5, 2024 finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered certain remedies. The order is subject to further proceedings and to appeal by both the DOJ and Google; a reversal could impose remedies such as prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution, which could materially harm Apple's search licensing revenue.

**October 2025 — Epic Games appeal**
The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments on an expedited basis on Apple's appeal of the district court's April 30, 2025 decision (Apple's request to stay the decision pending appeal had been denied, but the court agreed to expedited consideration).

Note: the filing also mentions that Apple settled certain ordinary-course matters "during the fourth quarter of 2025" without material impact, but this is tied to a fiscal quarter rather than a specific calendar day or month, and all other dated events in these disclosures (e.g., the March 21, 2024 DOJ complaint, the 2024 ECJ State Aid ruling) fall outside calendar 2025.

Pfizer's 2021 Form 10-K quantifies the Upjohn separation costs in two places, with figures stated as follows:

**1. MD&A — Overview of Our Performance, Operating Environment, Strategy and Outlook (p. 32):**

The filing states: *"We expect to incur costs of approximately $700 million in connection with separating Upjohn, of which, approximately 75% has been incurred since inception and through December 31, 2021. These charges include costs and expenses related to separation of legal entities and transaction costs."*
- **"approximately 75%"** — the portion of that expected total incurred since inception through December 31, 2021.

Based on NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 Form 10-K (year ended January 25, 2026), the filing explains that valuing non-marketable equity securities requires judgment for the following reasons:

**From Note 1 (Significant Accounting Policies):**
These are investments in privately-held companies that do not have a readily determinable fair value. They are measured at cost minus impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for an identical or similar investment in the same issuer (the "measurement alternative"). Fair value is based on observable inputs in an inactive market, and "the valuation requires our judgment due to the absence of market prices and inherent lack of liquidity."

**From Note 8 (Non-marketable Equity Securities):**
The securities are valued under the measurement alternative using valuation methods that rely on:
- Observable transactions for similar investments of the same issuer, and
- Unobservable inputs, specifically: volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and security-specific rights and obligations.

**From the Critical Accounting Estimates section of MD&A:**
The filing designates non-marketable equity securities as a critical accounting estimate — one involving "a significant level of estimation uncertainty" that "could have a material impact" on financial condition or results of operations. It notes the measurement-alternative adjustments "may require use of unobservable inputs," and that impairment is assessed quarterly based on qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee's operating performance and market trends.

In short, the filing attributes the complexity and judgment to the absence of market prices, the inherent lack of liquidity of private-company investments, the resulting reliance on unobservable valuation inputs (volatility, expected time to liquidity, risk-free rate, and security-specific rights and obligations), and the judgment involved in quarterly impairment assessments of investee performance and market trends.

I've reviewed the segment-reporting note in each of the eight filings, which is where the chief operating decision maker (CODM) is identified. Three of the eight identify the CODM as a group acting collectively; the other five name a single individual.

**Filings identifying the CODM as a group of executives acting collectively:**

1. **JPMorgan Chase — 2024 Form 10-K, Note 32 (Business segments & Corporate), p. 313**
   - Group name: the **Operating Committee**
   - Language: the business segments "reflect the manner in which financial information is evaluated by the Firm's Operating Committee, whose members act collectively as the Firm's CODM." The filing does not list the individual members or their titles in the note.

2. **Berkshire Hathaway — 2024 Form 10-K, Note 26 (Business segment data), p. K-108**
   - The group is given no name. The filing says only: "Berkshire's chief operating decision maker consists of the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, the Vice Chairman of Insurance Operations and the Vice Chairman of Non-Insurance Operations."
   - So its composition is three positions: the Chairman & CEO, the Vice Chairman of Insurance Operations, and the Vice Chairman of Non-Insurance Operations.

3. **ExxonMobil — 2024 Form 10-K, Note 18 (Disclosures about Segments and Related Information), p. 108**
   - Group name: the **Management Committee (MC)**
   - Language: "The MC is considered collectively, and not in their individual capacity, to be our Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM), and includes our CEO, CFO, and two Senior Vice Presidents serving as contact executives overseeing the Upstream and Product Solutions businesses."

**Filings identifying the CODM as a single individual (for contrast):**

- **NVIDIA fiscal 2024 10-K, Note 17 (Segment Information), p. 78:** "Our Chief Executive Officer, who is considered to be our chief operating decision maker"
- **Apple fiscal 2024 10-K, Note 13 (Segment Information and Geographic Data), p. 46:** refers to "the Company's chief operating decision maker" without identifying any person or group (elsewhere in the filing this is the CEO, but the note itself does not specify an individual or collective body)
- **Walmart fiscal 2024 10-K, Note 13 (Segments and Disaggregated Revenue), p. 78:** defines segments as those operations whose results "the chief operating decision maker ('CODM') regularly reviews" — the note does not name the person or group (Walmart's CODM is its CEO, but the note doesn't state this)
- **Pfizer 2024 10-K, Note 17 (Segment, Geographic and Other Revenue Information), p. 99:** "Pfizer's CODM is the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer"
- **Boeing 2024 10-K, Note 23 (Segment and Revenue Information), p. 114:** "Our chief operating decision maker is currently our President and Chief Executive Officer (CEO)"

A nuance worth noting: Apple's and Walmart's segment notes reference "the chief operating decision maker" in the singular-impersonal sense and do not describe the role as a collective group, so they do not fall into the category you asked about. Only JPMorgan (Operating Committee), Berkshire (an unnamed trio of the Chairman & CEO plus the Vice Chairmen of Insurance and Non-Insurance Operations), and ExxonMobil (Management Committee, composed of the CEO, CFO, and two Senior Vice Presidents) expressly identify the CODM as a collective body.

## Answer: Two of the eight filings qualify

### 1. Walmart — fiscal 2025 10-K (year ended January 31, 2025): sold JD.com

Note 8 (Fair Value Measurements) contains a subsection titled **"Sale of Investment"**:

> "In August 2024, the Company sold its investment in JD.com for net proceeds of approximately $3.6 billion and recorded a realized loss of $0.3 billion within other gains and losses."

The same note explains that the fair value of Walmart's equity investments "decreased $4.2 billion during fiscal 2025, primarily due to the sale of the Company's investment in JD.com in August 2024." August 2024 falls within Walmart's fiscal year ended January 31, 2025. JD.com was a publicly traded equity investment, not a subsidiary or operating business. Walmart had first disclosed its JD.com stake in 2016.

### 2. Pfizer — 2025 10-K (year ended December 31, 2025): sold Haleon

Note 2C (Equity-Method Investments) states:

> "We sold the remaining portion of our investment in Haleon for $6.3 billion and recognized a net loss on the sale of $144 million in the first quarter of 2025 in Other (income)/deductions––net."

Haleon plc is the London-listed consumer healthcare company (the former GSK/Pfizer consumer health joint venture). The filing details Pfizer's staged exit: roughly 30% of its stake sold in March 2024, another ~34% of the remainder in October 2024, and the final ~15% in Q1 2025. This was a financial investment, not a subsidiary or operating business — Pfizer separately divested operating assets (e.g., its rare-disease gene therapy portfolio to Alexion), but that is an asset sale, not a share sale.

## The other six filings do not qualify

- **Berkshire Hathaway (2025 10-K):** Note 6 reports $30.7 billion of equity security sales in 2025, but no company is named as having been fully exited. The only named investment actions are *impairments* of Kraft Heinz (~$5.0B) and Occidental (~$5.7B) — both positions were retained, not sold.
- **Apple (fiscal 2025 10-K):** Its portfolio consists of marketable debt/cash-management securities; there is no disclosure of selling all shares of any named company.
- **NVIDIA (fiscal 2025 10-K):** Note 7 reports $88 million of net realized gains on publicly held equity securities sold in fiscal 2025, but no investee company is named.
- **JPMorgan Chase (2025 10-K):** Named equity items are Visa-related — 2024 share-exchange gains and a 2024 donation of Visa C shares (prior-year events); JPMorgan still holds restricted Visa B-2 shares at year-end 2025, so there was no 2025 full exit of a named investment.
- **ExxonMobil (2025 10-K):** Note 19 (Divestment Activities) describes sales of "businesses, affiliates, facilities, and conventional or unconventional assets" (Singapore, Argentina, France, U.S., Nigeria, etc.) — operating businesses and assets, which your question expressly excludes — not a named company's shares held as an investment.
- **Boeing (2025 10-K):** Its major 2025 disposition was the sale of portions of its Digital Aviation Solutions business (Jeppesen, ForeFlight, AerData, OzRunways) to Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion — an operating business sale, which is excluded. Its named equity-method investments (e.g., United Launch Alliance) were retained.

**Bottom line:** Of the eight fiscal 2025 filings, only **Walmart's** (JD.com) and **Pfizer's** (Haleon) report that the company sold all of its remaining shares in another named company held as an investment during that fiscal year.

I now have the complete picture from the filing. Here are the amounts Berkshire's 2025 Form 10-K reports for its other-than-temporary impairment (OTTI) losses on the two equity-method investments:

## 1. Kraft Heinz — approximately $5.0 billion (pre-tax)

From Note 5 (Equity method investments) to the Consolidated Financial Statements:
- "In the second quarter of 2025, we recorded a **pre-tax** impairment loss of approximately **$5.0 billion** on our investment in **Kraft Heinz** common stock as a component of our equity in the earnings of Kraft Heinz, which reduced the carrying value of our investment to fair value based on the quoted market price."

## 2. Occidental Petroleum — approximately $5.7 billion (pre-tax)

From Note 5:
- "We also recorded a **pre-tax** impairment loss of approximately **$5.7 billion** on our investment in **Occidental** common stock in the fourth quarter of 2025 as a component of our equity in the earnings of Occidental, which reduced the carrying value of our investment to fair value based on the quoted market price at that time."

## 3. After-tax equivalents (from the MD&A "Other" earnings table footnote, p. K-54)

The footnote to the after-tax other earnings table states the equity method earnings line:
- "* Excludes other-than-temporary impairment losses on investments in **Kraft Heinz of $3.76 billion** and **Occidental of $4.50 billion**." — these are the **after-tax** amounts corresponding to the two pre-tax charges above.

## Amounts specifically excluded, per your criteria

- **Berkshire's $2.4 billion share of Kraft Heinz's own impairment losses**: Note 5 states Berkshire's 2025 equity in Kraft Heinz earnings included Berkshire's proportionate share ($2.4 billion) of the after-tax intangible asset and goodwill impairment losses Kraft Heinz itself reported (~$8.7 billion) in its first nine months of 2025 — this is Kraft Heinz's own charge, not Berkshire's OTTI loss.
- **Basis differences**: The ~$5.0 billion excess of Berkshire's share of Kraft Heinz shareholders' equity over the equity-method carrying value (attributed to Kraft Heinz indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill), and the ~$3.4 billion excess of the Occidental carrying value over Berkshire's share of Occidental shareholders' equity — these are carrying-value-vs.-equity differences, not impairment losses.
- **Equity-method earnings figures**: The 2025 equity in earnings of Kraft Heinz (−$4,393 million) and Occidental (−$5,302 million) merely *include* the impairment losses and are not the impairment amounts themselves.

In short: Berkshire's own OTTI write-downs to quoted market value were **$5.0 billion pre-tax ($3.76 billion after-tax) for Kraft Heinz** (Q2 2025) and **$5.7 billion pre-tax ($4.50 billion after-tax) for Occidental** (Q4 2025).

## Background (Note 2, Fair value measurement)

On May 6, 2024, Visa accepted the Firm's tender of its 37.2 million Visa Class B-1 shares in exchange for a combination of Visa Class B-2 shares and Visa Class C shares. As of September 30, 2024, the Firm had disposed of all of its Visa C shares through sales in the second and third quarters of 2024 and through a contribution to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation in the second quarter of 2024. The retained ~18.6 million Visa B-2 shares are held in other assets at their nominal carryover basis because of transfer restrictions and conversion-rate uncertainty.

## Effects on 2024 financial results

1. **Net gain on Visa shares — $7.9 billion**, recorded in the second quarter of 2024 in other income (noninterest revenue), in the Corporate segment:
   - An **initial gain of $8.0 billion** based on the fair value of the Visa C shares received (Note 2; Note 6 shows a $7,990 million "Gain on Visa shares" in other income, relating to the initial gain on the Visa C shares).
   - The quarter also reflected other Visa-related activity — fair value changes of the Visa C shares and related derivative instruments, and dividends — which brought the net result to the **$7.9 billion net gain** (Three-Year Summary footnote; Executive Overview; Corporate segment results).

2. **Contribution of Visa shares to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation — $1.0 billion**, recorded in the second quarter of 2024 in other expense (noninterest expense), in the Corporate segment. This represented a portion of the Visa C shares.

3. **Revenue growth attribution**: The 23% increase in full-year noninterest revenue (to $85.0 billion) was "predominantly driven by" the $7.9 billion net Visa gain; likewise, Corporate noninterest revenue of $7.6 billion (vs. $132 million in 2023) and the 5% increase in firmwide noninterest expense both cite the Visa items as drivers (with amounts given).

4. **Effective tax rate**: The 2024 effective tax rate rose to 22.1% from 19.6%, driven in part by "changes in the mix of income and expenses... including the impact of the net gain on Visa shares and the contribution of Visa shares to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation" (no separate dollar amount is given for this tax effect). The Corporate segment tax discussion similarly attributes its $2.8 billion income tax expense in part to the Visa gain and contribution.

5. **Derivatives tied to prior Visa B share sales**: The notional amount of shares underlying derivative instruments (entered into with purchasers of Visa B shares sold before 2024, under which the Firm retains conversion-rate risk) was adjusted as a result of the exchange offer; as of December 31, 2024 these derivatives were associated with 11.6 million Visa B-2 shares. They are carried at fair value in trading liabilities, with changes in fair value recognized in other income (no specific 2024 gain/loss amount is stated).

## Effects on risk measures (Market Risk Management — VaR)

6. **Value-at-risk**: The receipt, holding and disposal of the Visa C shares was the predominant driver of a **$4 million increase in average Total VaR** for 2024 versus 2023 (to $47 million from $43 million, 95% confidence, one-day horizon). More specifically:
   - The Visa C shares caused **elevated average and maximum Corporate VaR, Other VaR and Total VaR** during the year — Corporate VaR averaged **$23 million with a maximum of $102 million** (vs. $12 million average / $17 million maximum in 2023), Other VaR averaged **$25 million with a maximum of $101 million**, and Total VaR reached a **maximum of $91 million**.
   - The increase and subsequent decline in daily Risk Management VaR observed in the second quarter of 2024 was primarily driven by changes in the Visa C share exposure in Corporate VaR.

No other risk measures (e.g., capital ratios, stress measures) are described as affected by the exchange, and no dollar amounts are given for effects beyond those listed above.
